paper_design_summary: University students were randomly assigned in a laboratory to brainstorm with another human or GPT-5-mini; the same recruited sample completed rubber-band alternative uses and chair improvements in random task order. Creativity researchers rated the resulting ideas for novelty and usefulness, coders counted ideas and categories, and additional output-coded analyses measured category convergence and semantic forward flow. The paper reports task-specific analyzed samples of 155 and 164 people, human-only comparisons, and whole-dyad comparisons that include AI output in HAI (pp. 8-10, 13-14, 17, 21-23, 39).

studies.label: Laboratory collaboration experiment: alternative uses and product improvement

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly assigned to human-human (HH) or human-AI (HAI) collaboration. Collaboration condition was between participants; the same recruited sample completed both tasks in random order. HH pairs drew lots for first speaker, whereas the human always spoke first in HAI. Random-sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described (pp. 8-10).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 155 people analyzed for AUT and 164 for PIT, not the unique union of people analyzed across the two tasks; the study-wide n_analyzed is therefore null. AUT excluded 14 people: 6 in HAI (4 instruction violations and 2 network failures) and 4 HH dyads (2 instruction violations and 2 network failures). PIT excluded 5 people: 1 HAI participant for network failure and 2 HH dyads (1 instruction violation and 1 network failure). Violations included producing more than one idea per turn, copying AI responses, only asking questions, or off-task chatting. Invalid data were removed for the affected task while valid data in the other task were retained (pp. 8-9, section 2.1). The overlap between task-specific exclusions is not reported.

ai_tool.how_used: Interactive turn-taking ideation partner through an API in a custom web chat interface, rather than unrestricted chatbot use. Human and AI alternated one idea per turn, with the human first; neither questions nor evaluations were permitted by the task instructions. The AI system prompt matched the human task and limited each AI idea to 40 Chinese characters. API calls were made from 2025/11/8 to 2025/12/21; printed settings: temperature = 0.70, top_p = 1.00, presence penalty = 0.00, frequency penalty = 0.20 (pp. 9–10, sections 2.2–2.3; pp. 42–43, Appendix 1).

task.description: Two task types in one experiment: Alternative Uses Task (AUT; divergent_test), generating novel, interesting, unusual uses for a rubber band; and Product Improvement Task (PIT; idea_generation), proposing creative ways to improve a chair. The single task-type field is other because neither task alone describes the experiment. Both used alternating concise ideas with the assigned partner. The later selection of the most creative idea was instructed, but no distinct scored selection outcome is reported (pp. 9-10, sections 2.2-2.3; pp. 42-44, Appendix 1).
task.duration: AUT 10 minutes; PIT 15 minutes; random order with a 3-minute break (p. 10, section 2.3).

outcomes.name: AUT: mean idea novelty
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two graduate students with creativity research backgrounds independently rated every idea's novelty using the Consensual Assessment Technique on a 7-point scale, blind to condition, identity, and hypotheses. Scores were averaged over raters and then over each person's ideas; AUT ICC = 0.88 (p. 13, section 2.5). Coded expert_raters because the paper explicitly describes their creativity research expertise. The participant unit refers to the human-role contrast from the linear mixed-effects role analysis (p. 14, section 2.6). The separately labeled dyad contrast aggregates the collaborating pair, including AI-authored ideas in HAI; its unit is team and its numbers must not be treated as human-only participant means. Parenthetical dispersion values in Tables 2 and 4 are copied exactly; the tables do not explicitly label them as SD or SE. APIM variants of this same outcome, including coefficients and SEs, appear in p. 19, Table 3; those associations condition on measured perspective taking and are not additional randomized treatments. The reported analyzed human sample for AUT is 155 people (p. 8, section 2.1); these are task-specific data from the same experiment. The paper does not specify the exact weighting used to combine members' novelty/usefulness scores into the dyad mean.

outcomes.name: AUT: immediate perspective-taking index (category convergence)
outcomes.question: with_ai

This measures convergence within the interacting dyad, not similarity among different independently working human participants; in HAI the comparison partner is AI. The paper calls perspective taking a process variable rather than a primary creativity outcome (p. 9, section 2.2). Parenthetical values in the dyad table are not explicitly labeled as SD or SE. eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met within the same laboratory experiment in the saved manuscript. The paper explicitly reports random assignment of participants to HH or HAI (p. 8, section 2.1), with GPT-5-mini available as an ideation partner during production and a human partner as the active comparison (pp. 9-10, sections 2.2-2.3). It reports 155 analyzed people for AUT and 164 analyzed people for PIT after task-specific exclusions (pp. 8-9, section 2.1); either task alone exceeds the 50-person threshold. These overlapping samples must not be added, and the unique analyzed total across tasks remains unknown. Independent creativity researchers rated generated ideas for novelty and usefulness, blind to condition and identity; scores were averaged over each participant's ideas (p. 13, section 2.5), and separate human-role contrasts are reported (pp. 17-18 and 22, sections 3.2.2 and 3.3.2). Thus the eligibility decision does not depend on AI-only output, self-reports, or the incompletely documented forward-flow analysis. Within-dyad convergence and forward flow remain other/with_ai process outcomes, and no after_ai creative-output assessment is reported. The open reporting and version questions do not unsettle any criterion in the saved full text.

one_line_finding: Humans collaborating with GPT-5-mini generated more novel ideas than humans collaborating with another person in AUT (d = 0.47, p = 0.029; p. 17, section 3.2.2) and PIT (d = 0.42, p = 0.045; p. 22, section 3.3.2).

Read all 814 markdown lines, including references and every appendix, then checked recorded counts, measurement numbers, effects, and locators against PDF text; Supplementary Figure 1 was also rendered in memory to check its human-role brackets. The paper designates novelty, usefulness, fluency, and flexibility as primary creative-performance outcomes without ranking tasks or endpoints (p. 9); paper_primary does not select multiple independent estimates for pooling. No preregistration is stated. Baseline creative potential, personality, collaboration tendency, general perspective-taking tendency, AI experience, and posttask self-reports are excluded because they are not scored creative outputs. Idea selection is instructed but no separate scored selection outcome is reported. APIM analyses in Tables 3 and 5, Supplementary Table 1, and Figures 4 and 7-10 are conditional associations involving the same creativity outcomes, not new randomized interventions; perspective taking was not manipulated (p. 34). Supplementary Table 2 contains model-fit statistics. Pure AI-role comparisons are not separate human-assistance studies. Delayed perspective taking refers to prior turns within the current task and does not imply delayed assessment or AI removal. No public data/code URL or external participant reuse is stated. Differences count substantive additions, omissions, coding choices, and aggregation choices, not synonymous wording, reordered statistic labels, or outcome renumbering. Remaining uncertainties shared by both forms are documented in open_questions; n_unresolved counts unresolved reconciliation entries.
